newsitem.title: USA: CPFL seen simple kick-off to Brazil utilities sale.
newsitem.headline: CPFL seen simple kick-off to Brazil utilities sale.

text.p: The sale of utility Companhia Paulista de Forca e Luz (CPFL) should be a straightforward kick-off for the multibillion-dollar sale of power companies owned by Brazil's Sao Paulo state, an adviser to the privatization said Wednesday.
Francisco Gros, a Morgan Stanley director helping coordinate the sale of CPFL and two other big Sao Paulo-owned power companies, said CPFL should be sold by the end of the year.
"CPFL is the most urgent, it's the simplest" of the three companies being sold, Gros said in a Reuter interview.
"It's a fairly simple, clear-cut distribution company with very few long-line transmissions."
He said CPFL's controlling shareholder, generator Companhia Energetica de Sao Paulo SA (CESP), wanted to sell CPFL to help pay off its debt quickly.
Gros, a former Brazilian Central Bank president, said CESP had short-term debt of $1.6 billion and long-term debt of $4.7 billion at the start of May.

Sao Paulo state, Brazil's industrial powerhouse, is also selling CESP and distributor Eletropaulo. Although no price has been set, state officials have put the total net worth of the three companies at $18 billion.
CPFL will be the first company privatized, with the rest expected to be sold perhaps in the next two years, Gros said.
Among key questions facing Morgan Stanley and SBC Warburg, the co-lead advisers on the privatizations, is how to sell off CPFL and other companies to get Sao Paulo the best price.
Prospective models included the companies' sales to a strategic operator or through a stock offering, Gros said.
The potentially most lucrative way is to transfer management control to a private operator along with a block of shares, then sell the rest of the shares when the company has been turned around.
"The problem here is I don't think that will be the model that will prevail, because Sao Paulo is in a hurry," Gros said.

Under Sao Paulo state law aimed at keeping the privatized utilities from gaining monopolies, CPFL has to be broken into three companies, Eletropaulo into as many as seven and CESP into "a large number," Gros said.
